title: Vortex-Beam-Driven Dirac Materials: Impurity and Polarization Effects on Light-Induced Vortex and Edge States
authors: Trevor W. Walsh, Eric E. Caldwell, Nancy P. Sandler, Mahmoud M. Asmar
abstract: We study impurity scattering and polarization detuning in finite-size vortex-light-beam-driven massive Dirac systems. In finite geometries, circularly polarized vortex light opens a dynamical gap where topological edge states coexist with photoinduced multiply quantized vortex states. We analyze how finite-size effects, vorticity, and effective particle-hole symmetry manifest in the quasienergy spectrum, real-space states, and local density of states. We show that angular-momentum mixing due to localized impurities and impurity clusters reshape vortex states, while when produced by circular polarization, it leads to a gradual filling of the dynamical gap with bulk-derived states. Our results indicate that both vortex and edge signatures remain observable in the presence of impurities and realistic polarization deviations, providing guidance for experimental realizations.
summary: This theoretical study investigates the stability of vortex and edge states in Dirac materials driven by structured light beams. By treating impurities and polarization deviations perturbatively, the authors show that while these imperfections break ideal symmetries, the fundamental topological signatures remain observable. The work provides critical guidance on realizing such systems experimentally.
main_problem: The study investigates how impurity scattering and polarization detuning affect light-induced vortex and edge states in finite-size, massive Dirac materials driven by a Vortex Light Beam (VLB). The goal is to understand the robustness of these topological features under realistic imperfections.
main_result: Both vortex and edge state signatures remain observable despite impurities and deviations from perfect circular polarization. Polarization detuning causes bulk states to gradually fill the dynamical gap via second-order level repulsion, while off-center impurities break rotational symmetry by mixing angular momentum sectors.
method: The analysis employs Floquet theory applied to a time-dependent Dirac Hamiltonian, solving for quasienergy spectra and real-space wavefunctions using numerical methods adapted for finite geometries. Perturbative corrections are calculated for both impurity potentials and polarization detuning terms.
model_or_system: The system is a 2D massive Dirac material ($H_D$) irradiated by a VLB, leading to a time-periodic Floquet Hamiltonian ($	ext{H}_F$). The analysis incorporates perturbations from static Gaussian impurities and polarization detuning ($\lambda$), which modifies the effective Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Quasienergy spectrum ($\epsilon_m$), real-space probability density ($ho(r)$), Local Density of States (LDOS), and spectral gap closing/filling.
important_parameters: Vortex Orbital Angular Momentum ($\ell$), polarization detuning ($\lambda$), impurity strength ($V_0$) and spatial extent ($a_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a perturbative approach for both impurities and detuning, assuming the topological edge states remain resolvable. It also relies on specific symmetry constraints (e.g., total angular momentum conservation in ideal cases).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the VLB incidence profile, the quasienergy spectrum showing gap opening/closing with $\ell$ or $\lambda$, and real-space probability densities demonstrating state localization and charge redistribution patterns due to impurities.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the ideal Floquet system (vortex/edge states) to analyzing perturbations. It first examines impurity effects, showing angular momentum mixing; then, it analyzes polarization detuning, revealing second-order gap filling via bulk state hybridization; finally, it synthesizes these findings to show robustness.
why_interesting: This work bridges topological physics (Dirac materials, edge states) with non-equilibrium quantum optics (Floquet engineering). The detailed analysis of how symmetry breaking mechanisms (impurities, detuning) affect quantized light-matter interactions is highly relevant for designing robust quantum devices.
